thread.title: Advice on bagging a truck
thread.first_post_html:
If everyone could, give your opinion on different bag setups. I've noticed a ton of bag questions, many of which are the exact same. If a mod could sticky this, it would be great.


My advice:

For the rear, the KP Components bolt on 4 link with cantilever attachment rides great. I, as well as many others, love this kit. The difficulty of the install was prolly a 6 out of 10, due to grinding a ton of rivits. You basically need regular hand tools, such as a grinder, drill with a step bit,a jack, jackstands, socket wrenches, box end wrenches, and a BFH. www.kpcomponents.com

For compressors, I am running the Air Commander, which consists of a York 209 compressor, which was used on older fords for the A/C. The kit comes with everything to hook the compressor up:mounting brackets, clutch, pressure switch, fittings, airline, check valve, water/oil trap, etc. The install was very straight forward, with a difficulty of about 4 out of 10. I had to modify my mounting brackets a little to fit, but no biggie. The compressor is made by Airlift. www.airliftcompany.com

For bags on the back I am running the Airlift 2b7 1/2" port bags. They feel great on the KP kit.

For valves, I am having great luck with (8) 3/8" smc valves. They are very quick.

For a tank, I am using the Airlift 8.5 gallon, which mounts under my bed, and doesnt hang below the rollpan. I have enough room to mount 2 under the bed on my obs.

For the front end, I recommend the Air Ride coolride setup, which consists of the tubular uca's and lca's to correct balljoing angles. It also has the cups, bolt on brackets for shocks, the shocks, and bags. I do not own the kit, but hopefully I will one day. I'd say the difficulty of this is about a 5 out of 10, using basic hand tools.

Up front, I am using cups from www.innovativeairsuspension.com Slam Specialties RS-72 bags, and homemade shock mounts with bilstein shocks. The front end rides very nice with this setup. I also have 2" spindles. I have not notched the frame for tierods, so I'm 1.5" from laying out up front.

Everyone add what you think is appropriate.

K.P. components all the way for everything! Period! end of storie! Once you go steak, you cant go back to milk!

My setup is KP Components 6-link, its easy to install (bolts to the hanger locations for the leaf springs) provides 2x the lift and better ride. I am running SMC 1/2" valves with mufflers on the dumps (quiets it significantly, slows the drop down and helps with control).

I also have the Air Commander engine driven compressor, and I cant imagine any other way, my usually fill is from about 150-185 lasts less than 30 seconds. Its not as noisy, and doesnt drain the battery, if you add up the costs of 2 Viair compressors plus an Optima battery to handle the load, and less alternator life, you are at the cost of the kit.

For switches/gauges I have the Dakota Digital ARC-1004 (similar to RidePro e) which is a digital guage with buttons on the gauge for the switches, I also have the remote controls, which I highly recommend as the guage only works when the truck is turned on.

Also, I recommend have a schroder valve on the tanks so that you can fill it up if your compressors have problems or you cant start your truck.

I can do the install but can I get the parts I need for this much? Are there any cheaper alterantives? I am building this as a learning experience and only plan to keep my truck a year or so and get something newer. If I have to fabricate some stuff it is not a big deal as I am a GM tech but I do not want to have to start from scratch.
BTW, it's a 93 GM ext cab sb. 2/4 drop right now.

check out some sites like www.suicidedoors.com for your parts or www.innovativeairsuspension.com. There's also a site called EAI, but i forget their address, just google it. suicidedoors makes it pretty affordable to bag your ride.

You should be able to do a full bag setup at around $2000-$2500 if you install it yourself. The parts for mine minus the gauges/switches (basic ones are around $150) and compressor was around $2000, and thats with the 6link and a slight markup on some of the parts.

So let me get this straight. The KP 6 link is $1170 and about another $150 for bags, Air Commander is $875, Easy Street front system is $635 including bags. That's $2855 right there. Valves, switches, tank, lines, fittings have to run at least $500 for a basic system. That comes to $3355 (or way over my budget) Are these guys giving 25% discounts to get me into my price range or am I screwed before I start?

I bagged my 04 using Kp 4 link and cantilever with firestone bags out back. Instead of grinding the rivet head off, take a drill near the same size and drill the center untill you are almost through the head. then take a punch and hammer and knock the stem through. The Kp kit works and rides great, I've only but 7K miles on it so far I hope my luck keeps up.

I used ART's upper and lower control arms up front along with there cups and firestone bags. The upper shock mount is best to be welded on. Mine pulled the bolts from the frame. I'm using ART's bigred valves with 3/8" ports and 1/2" line. I'm upgrading now to 3 5 gallon tanks under my bed (if they all will fit) and a air commander. Before this I had one 5 gallon tank and a Viair 450. I grew to hate the noise that thing makes with in a week on installing it. 5 gallons of air is not enough to raise to front and rear of the truck. lift front to ride height and raise rear about halfway then wait for tank to refill.

For guages I'm using once again ART's ridepro E it's a small selfcontained unit that has the guages and switches all in one. I have it mounted in my over head console. It's easy to read and use. plus you can upgrade to a remote. I plan on doing some time down the road.

rewrite.summary: This thread discusses various setups for bagging trucks, including rear kits, compressors, front ends, and budgets. Users share their experiences and recommendations.
seo_outline: Rear Bagging Kits: KP Components Bolt-on 4-Link with Cantilever Attachment
Compressors: Air Commander by Airlift Company
Bags for the Rear: Airlift 2b7 1/2" Port Bags
Front End Setup: Air Ride Coolride Kit with Slam Specialties RS-72 Bags and Bilstein Shocks
rewrite.rewritten_article_markdown:
When considering bagging a truck, the community recommends several key components that can significantly enhance your vehicle's performance and comfort. Here are some top setups based on user recommendations.

### Rear Bagging Kits
Many users recommend the **KP Components Bolt-on 4-Link with Cantilever Attachment** as it offers great ride quality and a moderate difficulty level for installation, estimated at around 6 out of 10 due to grinding rivets. ([Post ID: 3694], [Post ID: 3708])

### Compressors
For the compressor setup, the **Air Commander** from Airlift Company is popular. It consists of a York 209 compressor that comes with all necessary components such as mounting brackets, clutch, pressure switch, fittings, airline, check valve, and water/oil trap. The installation difficulty is about 4 out of 10. ([Post ID: 3694])

### Rear Bags
Airlift's **2b7 1/2" Port Bags** are favored for their great performance with the KP kit. ([Post ID: 3694])

### Valves
**SMC 3/8” Quick Response Valves** have been highly recommended by users due to their quick responsiveness and ease of use. ([Post ID: 3694])

### Air Tanks
An **Airlift 8.5 Gallon Tank** is suitable for most setups, especially when mounted under the bed or near the roll pan to avoid hanging below. ([Post ID: 3694], [Post ID: 3708])

### Front End Setup
For the front end, the **Air Ride Coolride Kit** with **Slam Specialties RS-72 Bags** and homemade shock mounts using Bilstein shocks is suggested for a comfortable ride. The installation difficulty is around 5 out of 10. ([Post ID: 3694])

post_rewrites.rewritten_content:
If possible, share your experiences and recommendations on different bag setups. A sticky thread by a moderator would be great.

For the rear end, the KP Components bolt-on 4-link with cantilever attachment performs exceptionally well. The installation difficulty rates around a 6 out of 10 due to extensive rivet grinding. Regular hand tools are required, including a grinder, drill with step bit, jack, jackstands, socket wrenches, box-end wrenches, and a BFH.

For compressors, I use the Air Commander kit from Airlift, featuring a York 209 compressor. The package includes mounting brackets, clutch, pressure switch, fittings, airline, check valve, water/oil trap, etc. Installation is straightforward with a difficulty level of about 4 out of 10. Minor modifications to the mounting brackets were necessary.

For rear bags, I use Airlift 2B7 1/2" port bags, which complement the KP kit well. For valves, (8) 3/8" SMC valves provide excellent performance and quick response.

For a tank, an Airlift 8.5-gallon model mounts under the bed without hanging below the roll pan. Room allows for mounting two tanks beneath the bed on my OBS.

In the front end, I recommend the Air Ride Coolride setup with tubular UCA's and LCA’s to correct ball joint angles. The kit includes cups, bolt-on brackets for shocks, shocks, and bags. Installation difficulty is approximately 5 out of 10 using basic hand tools. For now, I use Innovative Air Suspension cups, Slam Specialties RS-72 bags, homemade shock mounts with Bilstein shocks, and 2-inch spindles. Frame notching for tie rods has been avoided, leaving me 1.5 inches from laying out the frame.

Share your thoughts!

I recommend the KP kit; it's a great value. I use firestones, which perform well. I installed shockwaves in the front and am very satisfied with their ride quality and ease of installation. Removal and replacement take about 30 minutes, provided you can remove your existing shocks.
Please share your suggestions on what would be most helpful for newcomers.

- Valves

Fittings and air lines:

- DOT line; good selection available at [http://www.suicidedoors.com/products/dot_airline.htm] and [http://www.innovativeairsuspension.com/site.htm]
K.P. components are the best choice for all applications. Once you use them, you won't want to switch. Steak is irreplaceable once you've tried it.

My setup includes KP Components 6-link lift, which provides twice the lift and an improved ride, mounting easily to the leaf spring hanger locations. I use SMC 1/2" valves with mufflers on the dumps, significantly reducing noise and improving control.

For air management, I have an Air Commander engine-driven compressor, as it is the most efficient option for my needs. Typically, my fill lasts between 150-185 seconds, taking less than 30 seconds to complete. This setup is quieter and doesn't drain the battery, making it a cost-effective alternative compared to using two Viair compressors or an Optima battery.

I use the Dakota Digital ARC-1004 gauge, which offers both digital readouts and switch functionality on the gauge itself. Remote controls are highly recommended as they allow operation even when the truck is off. Additionally, I recommend installing a Schroeder valve on the air tanks for backup in case of compressor failure or if starting the truck proves difficult.

Certainly. You're looking for ways to perform a functional brake fluid swap system (FBSS) on your 1993 GM extended-cab SB truck with a 4-link and spindles, aiming to stay under $2500 and minimize frame deformation. Given your experience as a GM technician, you're willing to fabricate some parts if necessary. Would this budget allow you to obtain the required components? Are there any cheaper alternatives available? You plan to build this project for learning purposes and intend to keep the truck for about a year before upgrading to a newer model.

Consider visiting websites like Suicide Doors (www.suicidedoors.com) and Innovative Air Suspension (www.innovativeairsuspension.com) for parts. You can also find EAI by searching online; while I forget the specific URL, they offer competitive pricing for customizing your vehicle.

A full bag setup can be installed yourself for approximately $2000 to $2500. My setup, excluding basic gauges/switches ($150) and compressor, cost around $2000, including a 6-link and slight markup on some parts.

The KP 6 link costs $1,170 with an additional $150 for bags. The Air Commander is priced at $875, and the Easy Street front system totals $635 including bags. This brings the initial cost to $2,855. Valves, switches, tank, lines, and fittings alone will run at least $500 for a basic setup. Therefore, the total comes to $3,355, which exceeds my budget significantly. Are these prices with discounts, or am I over预算了？

You are selecting premium components for a budget-friendly installation. Consider substituting the KP kit with Suicidedoors 4-link and brackets ($450), the Aircommander with a single Viair 450 ($200), and the Easy Street front with bags, cups, and shocks from Innovative ($350). This will free up significant funds for essential items like rear shocks, rear airbags, and additional parts needed during installation.
Yes, affordable shoes can perform just as well as more expensive ones.
This is very informative. Thank you.

We installed front air suspension on a '99 vehicle using Airlift 2B7 bags at $65 each, Innovative cups for $50 per pair, 4 used Blitzluft valves for $125 on eBay, an 8.5-gallon Airlift tank for $55, a Viair 450 compressor for $200, compression fittings for the front for $90, and a KP gauge for $30. Additionally, we purchased 50 feet of 1/2-inch line for $30 and 20 feet of 1/8-inch line for $5.

I installed a KPX4 link and cantilever setup with Firestone bags at the rear of my 2004 model truck. To remove the rivet, drilling nearly through it with a drill of similar size and then using a punch to push the stem through worked effectively. The KPX kit performs well, though I've only put about 7,000 miles on it so far; I hope my luck continues.

For the front suspension, I used ART's upper and lower control arms along with their polyurethane bushings and Firestone bags. The upper shock mount needed welding to the frame, as mine pulled out the bolts over time. I am now upgrading to three 5-gallon tanks under the bed (assuming they fit) and an Air Commander system; previously, I had one 5-gallon tank and a Viair 450 that was noisy after only a week.

To raise the truck, I lifted the front to ride height and raised the rear halfway, waiting for the tanks to refill. For gauges, I am using ART's RidePro E again, a compact self-contained unit with integrated gauges and switches mounted in the overhead console; it is user-friendly and can be upgraded to a remote.

I plan to continue improving my setup in the future.
